result.summary: Jove lets the gods join the war on whichever side they please, and they take positions around Troy while Apollo pushes Aeneas to face Achilles. Neptune rescues Aeneas from certain death, and Achilles then cuts down many Trojans, while Apollo and Minerva protect Hector.

scenes.title: Council of the gods
scenes.summary: Jove calls the gods to Olympus and allows them to join either side. They go down to the battlefield.
scenes.stakes: Achilles might overturn fate and sack Troy before its appointed time.

scenes.title: The gods clash
scenes.summary: Strife rises, the earth shakes and Hades fears for his realm. The gods line up against each other and Apollo stirs Aeneas.
scenes.stakes: Hades fears his hidden halls will be laid bare to mortals and immortals.

scenes.title: Apollo urges Aeneas on
scenes.summary: Apollo, disguised as Lycaon, shames Aeneas into fighting. Juno and Neptune decide to watch from the barrow of Hercules.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas risks death against a stronger hero.

scenes.title: Achilles and Aeneas duel
scenes.summary: The two heroes trade boasts, and Aeneas recites his lineage. Their spears are thrown, and Achilles' god-made shield holds.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas faces death at Achilles' hands, and Achilles risks being struck down in turn.

scenes.title: Neptune saves Aeneas
scenes.summary: Neptune argues with Juno, then hides Achilles' sight and carries Aeneas away. Achilles rallies the Achaeans.
scenes.stakes: Aeneas must live because fate has chosen his line to rule the Trojans.

scenes.title: Hector escapes Achilles
scenes.summary: Hector rallies the Trojans but Apollo warns him off. After Polydorus falls, Hector attacks, but Minerva and Apollo save him.
scenes.stakes: Hector would die at Achilles' hands.

scenes.title: Achilles' slaughter
scenes.summary: Achilles kills many Trojans, comparing his fury to wildfire.

alias_notes.explanation: The river is called Scamander by men and Xanthus by the gods.
Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.
Apollo takes the voice and likeness of Lycaon son of Priam.

notable_quotes.reason: Achilles' proverb that even a fool learns after the event.
Aeneas on how freely the tongue can run in any direction.
Foretells that Aeneas and his descendants will rule the Trojans.

analysis.text: Fate and divine will pull against each other: Jove fears Achilles may override fate, and Neptune saves Aeneas because his line is destined to survive.
Aeneas's prophecy of rule reflects traditions of Troad ruling families claiming descent from Aeneas, later used by Rome.

legacy.text: Aeneas's survival here underpins Virgil's Aeneid, where he founds the line leading to Rome.

fun_facts.text: Achilles' shield has five layers: two bronze, two tin, and one gold.

language_notes.text: "Round you, O son of Peleus" addresses Achilles directly; Achaeans is Homer's common name for the Greeks.
"Many-delled" means having many hollows or glens; it describes the folds of Mount Olympus.
Rivers and nymphs attend as divinities; Oceanus, the great world-encircling river, alone stays away.
"Lord of the earthquake" is Neptune's epithet, as god of the sea and earthquakes.
"Override fate itself" means Achilles might exceed what destiny has allowed, taking Troy before its appointed time.
"Plying lustily" means moving vigorously; Vulcan is lame, yet his thin legs work hard.
"Held themselves aloof" refers to Jove's earlier ban on the gods joining the fighting; now he allows them to take sides.
Acropolis means the high fortified citadel of a city; here it is Troy's citadel, Pergamus.
"Mouldy mansions" means the damp, decaying halls of the underworld.
Scamander, called Xanthus by the gods, is a river god; the poem often notes that gods and men use different names for things.
"Glut" means to feed to excess; Achilles wants to satisfy Mars with Hector's blood.
Lycaon, a son of Priam, was killed by Achilles earlier, so Apollo borrows the voice of a dead man.
"Vaunted" means boasted. Aeneas had boasted at a feast, over wine, that he would face Achilles.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted; "fly" here means flee, not take wing.
"Guardian angel" is the translator's Christian-flavoured phrase for a protecting deity; Homer has no angels.
Fate was imagined as spinning a thread of life for each person at birth, so Achilles' fate is already fixed.
"Out of the beaten track" means away from the main fighting, in a place apart.
Refers to an earlier story: Hercules was chased by a sea-monster sent by Neptune, and the Trojans built him a refuge.
"To wit" is an old formula meaning "that is to say," introducing the names of the two champions.
"Demesne" means an estate of land; "passing richness" means surpassing richness.
Lyrnessus was a city near Troy that Achilles sacked earlier in the war, taking Briseis there as captive.
A proverb: even fools understand a thing only after it has happened, when it is too late.
Boreas is the North Wind, here imagined as a stallion mating with the mares.
Ganymede was a Trojan prince taken to Olympus to serve wine to the gods.
"Gainsaid" means contradicted: whatever one man says, another can answer with the opposite.
"Fain" means eager or willing.
"Pelian ash" refers to the ash-wood spear from Mount Pelion, given to Peleus.
Apollo had urged Aeneas to face Achilles, so Neptune calls him a fool for heeding the god's advice.
"The son of Saturn" is Jove (Zeus), who would be angry if Aeneas, whom he favours, were killed.
Dardanus, son of Jove, was ancestor of the Trojan royal line; Aeneas descends from him, so his survival preserves the line.
"Earth-shaker" is Neptune's epithet, as god of earthquakes and the sea.
The Cauconians were allies of Troy, here shown arming at the edge of the battle.
"Let him go hang" is a colloquial dismissal, meaning Achilles no longer cares about Aeneas.
"Clip short" means cut off or leave unfinished: Hector claims Achilles will not fully carry out his boasts.
"Vaunted" means boasted or exulted over a defeated enemy.
"You be low" is a pun-like taunt: "lie low" in death, far from the rich estate Achilles names.
The King of Helice is Neptune, the earth-shaker, who was honored with bull sacrifices; a bellowing bull was thought to please him.
"The lap of heaven" means the issue rests with the gods, beyond human control.
"Hound" is a strong insult, implying shamelessness and cowardice.
"Stayed" means stopped or brought down; Achilles cripples Demouchus with a knee wound before finishing him.
Clasping the knees was the ritual gesture of a suppliant begging for mercy, which Achilles here refuses.
"Forbearance" means restraint or willingness to spare an enemy.
"Marrow" here refers to spinal matter, a typical graphic detail of Homeric battle description.
"Tread" means thresh: oxen were driven over cut barley to trample out the grain.
"Bedrabbled" means splattered and soiled; "tyres" are the metal rims of the chariot wheels.

context_notes.text: Themis is the goddess of order and custom, so she fittingly acts as Jove's herald to summon the gods.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) is the divine smith who builds the gods' houses and arms.
Juno, Minerva, Neptune, Mercury and Vulcan all favour the Achaeans; Juno and Minerva hate Troy.
Mars, Apollo, Diana, Leto, Xanthus (a river god) and Venus side with the Trojans.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) supports the Achaeans; Strife is a personified spirit of war.
The sire of gods and men is Jove (Zeus); Neptune (Poseidon) is his brother and god of the sea and earthquakes.
Apollo, Diana, Leto and Mercury here side with Troy or oppose Achaean-favoring gods; Vulcan is the smith god of fire.
Achilles raided the region around Mount Ida earlier in the war, sacking Lyrnessus and Pedasus; the Lelegae were allies of Troy.
Venus (the Greek Aphrodite) was Aeneas' mother, by Anchises. Apollo uses her divine parentage to claim Aeneas outranks Achilles.
Thetis, Achilles' mother, was a sea-goddess, daughter of the sea-god Nereus, called here the old man of the sea.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is the god of the sea and earthquakes; he favours the Greeks here but is cautious.
Priam was the aged king of Troy; Aeneas was his kinsman but not one of his sons.
Venus (Greek Aphrodite) is the goddess of love; Aeneas is her son, which is why gods tend to protect him.
Vulcan forged Achilles' new shield in Book 18, with five layers of metal.
Neptune, god of the sea and earthquakes, favoured the Greeks, yet here pities Aeneas, who is fated to survive.
Juno and Minerva (Greek Hera and Athena) favour the Greeks and swore an oath never to help Troy.
Hades is the god of the dead; his "house" is the underworld.
Apollo favored the Trojans and often protected Hector, who here is warned against facing Achilles directly.
Polydorus is Priam's youngest son. His father's ban on his fighting makes his death especially pitiable.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) supports the Greeks and Achilles, so she deflects Hector's spear.
Tros is a young Trojan; his appeal to equal age echoes Priam's later plea to Achilles and shows Achilles' mercilessness now.
Thrace, north of the Aegean, was a Trojan ally region famed for horses and fighters.

literary_notes.text: "Cloud-compelling" is a fixed epithet for Jove, evoking his power over storms and the sky.
"The blaze of battle" likens war to a fire about to be kindled.
Jove's fear that Achilles will storm the city anticipates the slaughter and Troy's coming fall.
Vulcan's limping yet lusty stride gives a vivid, slightly comic picture of the proud crippled god.
Achilles is likened to Mars, stressing his terrifying, godlike force in the Trojans' eyes.
Mars is compared to a black thunder-cloud, conveying his darkness, noise and menace.
Hades' terror at the cracking earth exaggerates the quake's power, showing how mighty the gods' conflict is.
Disguised Apollo goads Aeneas by recalling his boast, showing that Aeneas' pride and honour can be used to move him.
"Shepherd of his people" names Aeneas by his role as leader, stressing his duty to fight.
Gods are terrifying when seen openly; the plan to reassure Achilles by a god's voice risks frightening him instead.
The narrator suddenly addresses Phoebus directly, a traditional epic gesture that adds vividness and reverence.
The closing view of Jove commanding from above reminds us that the divine mortals' battles ultimately follow his control.
Achilles is compared to a lion roused by hunters, stressing his reluctant-seeming but terrible fury as he attacks.
Achilles ends his taunt with a bitter maxim, conveying contempt and warning that Aeneas will learn too late.
Aeneas exaggerates how many insults they could trade, saying a hundred-oared ship couldn't carry them.
The narrator reveals the shield's divine strength while Achilles fears it will fail, so the reader knows more than he does.
Neptune's question stresses Aeneas's innocence and the injustice of his suffering, persuading the other gods.
The darkness over Achilles' eyes and the spear laid at his feet show the god's intervention visibly.
Achilles' wide eyes and angry exclamation show his astonishment and quick temper.
Achilles claims even Mars or Minerva would shrink from such a fight, showing his boastful determination.
Valour is imagined as a garment Achilles wears, showing him wholly possessed by courage and fury.
Hippodamas's dying bellow is compared to a bull sacrificed to Neptune, making his death like a ritual slaughter.
Hector's charge is compared to a flame of fire, showing his sudden grief-driven fury; it echoes his earlier fire imagery.
"Thrice" and the fourth rush build suspense and show the gods' protection of Hector, a typical Homeric pattern of three attempts.
The narrator addresses Tros as "Fool", commenting with pity on his futile hope and signaling Achilles' changed, merciless temper.
Achilles' rage is compared to wildfire sweeping a dry forest, conveying destructive, uncontrollable force spreading in all directions.
Horses trampling bodies are likened to oxen threshing barley, turning a farm scene into an image of war's brutality.
Blood-spattered axle, rails and hands give a vivid visual picture of the carnage, ending on Achilles' relentless pursuit of glory.
